summary: Specifies requirements for features to add to the IETF Datatracker so working group chairs can enter and update the status of their Internet-Drafts. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The IETF's online tracker follows a document once it is sent for publication, but says nothing about a draft that a working group is still writing. This memo lists what the tracker would need so that a group's chair can record where each draft has got to, and so that everyone can see it.

questions: how to track wg drafts in datatracker
subtitle: Features needed for IETF working group chairs to track the state of their drafts in the Datatracker.

tldr.problem: The IETF Datatracker can follow a draft once it goes to the IESG for publication, but it has almost no ability to track the drafts a working group is still working on.
tldr.mechanism: The document specifies requirements for letting chairs and their delegates record a working group state, annotation tags and protocol writeups per draft, with an access model covering chairs, delegates, document shepherds and area directors.
tldr.outcome: The requirements are written to be optional and per draft, so a chair can use as much or as little of the tool as suits the group, and every change is logged with who made it and when.

today: RFC 6175 is an Informational document from March 2011, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes it and none that updates it. It is a list of requirements for a tool rather than a protocol, and the working group states it refers to are defined in RFC 6174.

sections.title: What the Datatracker Cannot Do Today
sections.content:
The IETF Datatracker is a web-based system for managing information about Internet-Drafts and RFCs, IPR disclosures, liaison statements and several other important aspects of the IETF process. It can track and report on the status of every draft that has been submitted to the IESG for evaluation and publication. In contrast, it currently has almost no ability to track the status of drafts that have not been submitted to the IESG.

Document authors and others have asked for more visibility into the status and progression of IETF Working Group drafts. This document specifies requirements to extend the Datatracker to enable status tracking and reporting for working group drafts, so that chairs can give everyone more information about the state of the drafts associated with their groups than is currently possible.

The document fixes its vocabulary first. The terms WG I-D, WG document and WG draft are used synonymously. A WG draft is a draft that has achieved consensus for adoption as a work item by a working group, as opposed to an individual submission draft that has not, or has not yet, achieved consensus. The terms do not apply to other material a working group reviews or produces: meeting materials such as Blue Sheets, agendas, jabber logs, scribe's notes, minutes and presentation slides are not WG documents in the sense of this document. The phrase WG status of an I-D refers to the working group state that a draft is in, as defined in RFC 6174, and not to the availability status such as Expired, Active or Replaced by, nor to the IESG states used by Area Directors.

An I-D associated with a working group means either a draft accepted as a WG draft, or one being considered under the guidance of a WG Chair for adoption. A draft whose filename contains the string draft-ietf- followed by a working group acronym is almost always a WG draft. A draft whose filename includes the author's name and a working group acronym but not the string -ietf- may be a candidate for adoption, and is also treated as associated with a working group.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of draft. One has been agreed by a working group and is being written; the other is a proposal someone has put forward for the group to adopt. The tracker knows about the first kind only once it reaches the publication queue. The memo defines which drafts count as belonging to a group, using the filename convention the IETF already follows.

sections.title: The General Requirements
sections.content:
The enhancements MUST be implemented so that WG Chairs and the people they designate as Delegates have the option to input and update the WG status of some, all or none of the drafts associated with their working groups, using the WG I-D states and I-D status annotation tags defined in RFC 6174 (R-001). The implementation must not require that chairs change their way of working, only provide optional features, and chairs must have the flexibility to track the status of their drafts as is most appropriate for them.

To ensure that at least some status information is tracked for every draft associated with a working group, the Datatracker must be enhanced to generate a few automatic state transitions for every WG draft, specified in a later section. Requirement R-001 SHALL NOT impair the ability of the Datatracker to track and display the availability state of any draft (R-002), such as Active, Expired or Replaces.

The Datatracker SHALL NOT permit users other than a working group's chairs to update the WG status of that group's documents through the regular interface, unless the privileges have been explicitly delegated by one of the group's chairs (R-003). The user interface given to chairs and delegates SHOULD have a look and feel similar to the interface used by Area Directors for drafts under formal evaluation by the IESG (R-004), and new pages SHOULD look like the existing pages for those drafts (R-005). New user interface code and style sheets SHOULD reuse or share existing code where practical, so that a change in the IESG status of a draft can benefit the WG status tracking and vice versa (R-006).

Every update to the WG status of a draft MUST be dated and timestamped, and that information MUST be usable when the status change history is displayed (R-007). The history MUST also identify the person or entity that made the update, such as a chair, a delegate, an AD, the system or the IETF Secretariat, and describe the change, for example that the WG state changed from one value to another or that an annotation tag was set or reset (R-008). Inputting or updating the WG status SHALL NOT overwrite any previously archived history: every update MUST be added to the status change history log (R-009). Tracking MUST be implemented per draft, not per working group (R-010), and SHOULD be implemented as a new front end to the existing IESG state machine (R-011). Authorized users SHALL be able to change the WG state of a draft independently from its IESG state and vice versa (R-012).
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are deliberately permissive. A chair can use the feature for one draft or for all of them. The tracker keeps two separate pieces of information, what the group thinks and what the IESG thinks, and lets each be changed on its own. Every change is logged with a timestamp and the name of whoever made it, and nothing in the log is ever overwritten.

sections.title: Who May Change What
sections.content:
Everyone needs to be able to view information about the WG status of a draft without logging on, so everyone is given read access to WG I-D status information (R-013). People who need to input, modify or update the status need write privileges, and must log on with a personal user id and password to get them (R-014).

After logging on, WG Chairs are given full read and write privileges to input and update the status information for all the drafts associated with their groups (R-015), and can choose from all the WG I-D states and status annotation tags defined in RFC 6174 to describe the current status (R-016). They may not create new states or state names (R-017), and may not change anything that is not related to the WG status, such as the IANA status, the RFC Editor status or the IESG status (R-018).

A Chair may designate a maximum of three people to act as Delegates for the drafts associated with each of their groups (R-019), and a maximum of three different people for a different group if they chair that one as well (R-021). The delegation MUST be to the individual identified by the login credentials used by the Datatracker at any given time rather than to an e-mail address (R-020), so that a person can change their e-mail address later without breaking the delegation. Chairs may designate people who hold other roles in the IETF process (R-022), review and change their Delegates (R-023), and input or upload Document Shepherd protocol writeups for all the drafts associated with their groups (R-024). They may designate themselves as Document Shepherds for some or all of the drafts (R-025), or designate other people (R-026), again by login credentials rather than by e-mail address (R-027), and must be warned in real time if the person they designate does not have the necessary login credentials (R-029), after which the Datatracker must let them confirm the original designee or pick another (R-030).

Delegates, such as WG Secretaries, have the same privileges as their chairs to input status information and protocol writeups (R-033). The Datatracker must send an e-mail to the chairs, the IETF Secretariat and a newly designated delegate who does not yet have a personal user id and password, so that the delegate can get one (R-034).

Document Shepherds need their own login (R-014). After logging on, they have restricted write privileges to upload or input protocol writeups for the WG drafts assigned to them, and only when those drafts are in the WG Consensus: Waiting for Writeup state (R-036). They can also set and reset the annotation tag called Doc Shepherd Followup Underway (R-037). Setting that tag indicates that work on the writeup has started; its absence or resetting may mean it has not started, has been put on hold, or has been completed.

An Area Director has the same privileges as a WG Chair to input and update WG status information and to designate Delegates and Document Shepherds (R-038), for every working group in their Area (R-039), while retaining their existing privileges over the IESG status of drafts (R-040). The Datatracker must make it easy for Area Directors to tell their IESG-level and WG-level privileges apart (R-041). The IETF Secretariat is involved in granting permissions, and before granting them to update WG status settings should verify that the person is a WG Chair or an AD, or has been delegated that authority (R-034, R-035).
sections.plainLanguage: Reading the status is open to anyone, but changing it needs a login. Chairs can change anything about their own groups' drafts, and can appoint up to three delegates per group to do it for them. Document shepherds get a narrower job: they can add the writeup for their draft once the group has agreed it is ready. Area directors have the chair's powers over every group in their area.

sections.title: Entering a Status: States, Tags and Writeups
sections.content:
The WG state of a draft may only be described using the states defined in RFC 6174. When a chair or delegate logs on to change the state, the Datatracker SHOULD display the current state of the draft, the length of time the document has been in its current state, the amount of time it may continue to remain there if that information is available, and the most likely next state or states (R-042). It MAY use the WG I-D state machine to identify the most likely next state (R-043). After displaying that information, the Datatracker SHALL make it easy to select a next state and to enter some text explaining the change for the history (R-044), and SHALL encourage the person to provide that context (R-045). The next state may be selected from the most likely ones or from any of the other states if a different change is needed (R-046).

Annotation tags may be used to describe a condition affecting a document, such as why it is in its current state, or to indicate an action needed to progress it. They do not change the state of the draft. Chairs and delegates SHALL be able to set and reset each of the tags defined in RFC 6174 for every draft associated with their groups (R-047), and tags SHALL be usable individually or in combination (R-048). When someone logs on to set or reset tags, the Datatracker SHOULD display a summary of all tag operations so far, and then guide the user to select the tags to set or reset (R-049). That summary SHALL also indicate when each tag was set or reset and who did it (R-050). More than one tag may be set or reset per logon, and the user should be encouraged to explain why (R-051).

The IESG currently requires a protocol writeup for every WG draft before the draft is submitted for evaluation. When a user logs on to input or upload a writeup, the Datatracker SHOULD make it easy to understand the current status of the writeup for every draft they are responsible for (R-052), and SHOULD indicate at least the date of the most recent writeup and the identity of the person who performed it (R-053). The Datatracker SHALL then provide an interface to input or upload a writeup and to set or reset the Doc Shepherd Followup Underway tag (R-054), and SHALL encourage the user to set or reset that tag before the end of each uploading session and to enter descriptive text (R-055). An e-mail goes to the author of the draft, copying the chairs and delegates, when the writeup is loaded, and a copy goes to the Document Shepherd if that is not the chair or delegate (R-056). If a Document Shepherd tries to upload a writeup for a draft that is not in the WG Consensus: Waiting for Writeup state, the Datatracker SHOULD warn that it may be too early and direct the shepherd to a chair for guidance (R-057). Chairs should be able to open the Document Shepherd interface without logging out and back in (R-058).
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of information can be entered. A state says where the draft is in the group's process, and the tool shows how long it has been there and what usually happens next. Tags add a note, such as why it is stuck, without moving it. A writeup is the technical record the group must produce before the draft can go for publication, and only its shepherd can file it.

sections.title: Automatic Changes, Timers and Notifications
sections.content:
To reduce the amount of information chairs and delegates have to enter, the tool must generate certain transitions automatically. A version-00 draft moves into the WG Document state when a WG Chair approves the posting of a draft whose filename includes the string -ietf- (R-070), and a draft transitions into the Submitted To IESG For Publication state at the same time that it is moved into the Publication Requested state in the IESG state machine by an AD or the IETF Secretariat (R-097).

Several states carry extra requirements. A draft in the Call for Adoption by WG Issued state has not yet achieved consensus in a group, and may only be moved there if it is not being considered elsewhere, has not been adopted by another group, has not expired and has not been withdrawn (R-059); it can only be in that state in one group at a time (R-060). Its state must not change until it expires, the chair moves it elsewhere, or the group declines to adopt it (R-060), in which case the chairs can cancel their interest in the draft (R-061) and the state becomes NULL in the WG state machine (R-062). A chair may set a maximum time the draft may remain in that state, expressed as a number of weeks, which MUST NOT extend beyond the expiry date of the draft (R-064, R-065), and the Datatracker must send an e-mail when that time runs out (R-067).

A draft moves into the Adopted by a WG state when the group agrees to adopt an individual submission, which may then take weeks or months to be resubmitted as a new version-00 WG draft (R-068). The WG Document state describes a draft that has been adopted and is being actively developed (R-069). A draft in the In WG Last Call state requires a chair to specify how long the last call will run, expressed as a number of weeks and not extending beyond the expiry date (R-083, R-084), the amount of time must be changeable afterwards (R-086), the tool must send a reminder when the time runs out (R-087), and a document may go straight into another last call (R-088). A draft in the WG Consensus: Waiting for Writeup state stays there until the chair moves it (R-089), and the Datatracker should be able to nudge the chairs to check on the shepherd's writeup after a set time (R-090).

Reporting has its own requirements. Anyone with write access must be able to get a summary of all status changes made to the drafts they are responsible for (R-098), and chairs should be able to get a summary of changes made on their behalf by their delegates (R-099). The Datatracker must send an e-mail to the authors of a draft and to the chairs and delegates of its group whenever the WG status is updated, giving the new state, the date of the change and who caused it (R-100). Everyone must be able to query the status of every document in a working group (R-101) and to search by author, state, intended maturity level or annotation tag (R-102).
sections.plainLanguage: Some changes happen on their own: when a group approves the first version of its draft, the tracker records it as a working document, and when the draft is sent for publication it records that too. Where time matters, such as a call for adoption or a last call, the chair sets a deadline and the tracker reminds them when it passes. Every change also sends an e-mail to the author.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document does not propose any new Internet mechanisms and has no security implications for the Internet. However, it contains specific requirements to add features to the IETF Datatracker to make it possible for a greater number of users to input or update status information about drafts associated with IETF working groups. Enhancing the Datatracker may create an opening for new denial-of-service attacks and for attempts by malicious users to corrupt the information in the WG document status database. The document does not propose any specific requirements to mitigate denial-of-service attacks on the Datatracker.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing on the Internet changes. The risk is to the tracker itself: letting more people write to it means more chance of a flood of requests or of someone entering false status, and the memo leaves those protections to the people who run the tool.

viz.caption: THE RULES THAT APPLY TO EVERYONE

items.title: Optional
items.text: Chairs may use the new features for some, all or none of their drafts, and need not change how they work.

items.title: Per draft, not per group
items.text: Status is tracked for each draft on its own, not for the group as a whole.

items.title: Two separate states
items.text: The group state and the IESG state of a draft can be changed independently of each other.

items.title: Nothing is overwritten
items.text: Every update is added to the history log; earlier history is never erased.

items.title: Every change is attributed
items.text: Each entry records the date, the person or system that made the change, and what the change was.

items.title: Availability status is untouched
items.text: The existing tracking of Active, Expired and Replaced is not impaired by any of this.

viz.caption: THE STATES A WORKING GROUP DRAFT CAN BE IN

items.title: Call for Adoption by WG Issued
items.text: A draft being considered for adoption. It has not yet achieved consensus in the group.

items.title: Adopted by a WG
items.text: An individual submission the group has agreed to take on as one of its own drafts.

items.title: WG Document
items.text: Adopted by the group and being actively developed.

items.title: Parked WG Document
items.text: Lost its author, or waiting for another document or a review to be completed.

items.title: Dead WG Document
items.text: Abandoned, though it may be resurrected if consensus is later reached.

items.title: In WG Last Call
items.text: Out for the group's final review, with a time limit that must be set.

items.title: WG Consensus: Waiting for Writeup
items.text: Development is finished and the protocol writeup is the last thing outstanding.

items.title: Submitted to IESG for Publication
items.text: Sent to the IESG, possibly back for revision.
